It is called each time a connection opens, before the password. Give `database` too, since it can no longer default to the user name. ```js const sql = postgres({ database: 'app', username: async () => (await secrets.get()).username, password: async () => (await secrets.get()).password }) ``` ### Password file With no password given, Postgres.js reads one from the file in `PGPASSFILE`, or `~/.pgpass` (`%APPDATA%\postgresql\pgpass.conf` on Windows), as libpq does: lines of `host:port:database:user:password`, where `*` matches anything and `\` escapes a `:` or `\`. On Unix the file is ignored unless only its owner can read it (`chmod 600`). ### SSL Although [vulnerable to MITM attacks](https://security.stackexchange.com/a/229297/174913), a common configuration for the `ssl` option for some cloud providers is to set `rejectUnauthorized` to `false` (if `NODE_ENV` is `production`): ```js const sql = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' ? // "Unless you're using a Private or Shield Heroku Postgres database, Heroku Postgres does not currently support verifiable certificates" // https://help.heroku.com/3DELT3RK/why-can-t-my-third-party-utility-connect-to-heroku-postgres-with-ssl postgres({ ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false } }) : postgres() ``` For more information regarding `ssl` with `postgres`, check out the [Node.js documentation for tls](https://nodejs.org/api/tls.html#tlsconnectoptions-callback). On Node.js an `ssl` object with a `ca` is made into one TLS context, which every connection made with that object shares, so a long `ca` list is parsed once rather than for each connection. Replacing one of its values, as with a renewed `cert`, makes a new context for the connections opened after that, but a change inside a value, such as a push onto the same `ca` array, is not seen. A `secureContext` given in the object is used as it is. The modes follow libpq's `sslmode`: `require`, `prefer` and `allow` encrypt without checking the certificate, and `verify-full` (or `sslrootcert=system` in the url) checks it against the system's certificate authorities. `prefer` and `allow` fall back to an unencrypted connection when the server has no TLS. Cloudflare Workers always check the certificate. #### Direct TLS PostgreSQL 17 and later can start TLS on the first byte instead of being asked first, which saves a round trip when connecting: ```js const sql = postgres('postgres://host/db?sslmode=require&sslnegotiation=direct') // or const sql = postgres({ ssl: 'require', sslnegotiation: 'direct' }) ``` On Node.js this is also the fastest encrypted connection, as it reads into the same shared buffer as a plain one. It needs a server that supports it, and is not available in Cloudflare Workers, whose sockets cannot send the ALPN it requires. #### Channel binding Over TLS, SCRAM authentication is bound to the server's certificate with SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS (`tls-server-end-point`) when the server offers it, so a man in the middle holding some other certificate that looks valid can't relay the login. `channel_binding` works as in libpq, and can also be given in the url or as `PGCHANNELBINDING`: - `'prefer'` (the default) binds when the server offers it, and authenticates as before when it doesn't. - `'require'` refuses any connection that isn't bound, so a server that isn't reached over TLS, doesn't offer it or authenticates without SCRAM is rejected with `CHANNEL_BINDING_REQUIRED`. - `'disable'` never binds. ```js const sql = postgres('postgres://host/db?sslmode=verify-full&channel_binding=require') ``` Certificates signed with Ed25519, for which binding isn't defined, are not bound. Cloudflare Workers sockets don't expose the server certificate, so there `'prefer'` doesn't bind and `'require'` is rejected. ### Multi-host connections - High Availability (HA) Multiple connection strings can be passed to `postgres()` in the form of `postgres('postgres://localhost:5432,localhost:5433', ...)`. This works the same as native the `psql` command. Read more at [multiple host URIs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/13/libpq-connect.html#LIBPQ-MULTIPLE-HOSTS). Connections will be attempted in order of the specified hosts/ports. On a successful connection, all retries will be reset. This ensures that hosts can come up and down seamlessly. If you specify `target_session_attrs: 'primary'` or `PGTARGETSESSIONATTRS=primary` Postgres.js will only connect to the primary host, allowing for zero downtime failovers. ### The Connection Pool Connections are created lazily once a query is created. This means that simply doing const `sql = postgres(...)` won't have any effect other than instantiating a new `sql` instance. > No connection will be made until a query is made. For example: ```js const sql = postgres() // no connections are opened await sql`...` // one connection is now opened await sql`...` // previous opened connection is reused // two connections are opened now await Promise.all([ sql`...`, sql`...` ]) ``` > When there are high amount of concurrent queries, `postgres` will open as many connections as needed up until `max` number of connections is reached. By default `max` is 10. This can be changed by setting `max` in the `postgres()` call. Example - `postgres('connectionURL', { max: 20 })`. This means that we get a much simpler story for error handling and reconnections. Queries will be sent over the wire immediately on the next available connection in the pool. Connections are automatically taken out of the pool if you start a transaction using `sql.begin()`, and automatically returned to the pool once your transaction is done. Any query which was already sent over the wire will be rejected if the connection is lost. It'll automatically defer to the error handling you have for that query, and since connections are lazy it'll automatically try to reconnect the next time a query is made. The benefit of this is no weird generic "onerror" handler that tries to get things back to normal, and also simpler application code since you don't have to handle errors out of context. There are no guarantees about queries executing in order unless using a transaction with `sql.begin()` or setting `max: 1`. Of course doing a series of queries, one awaiting the other will work as expected, but that's just due to the nature of js async/promise handling, so it's not necessary for this library to be concerned with ordering. Since this library automatically creates prepared statements, it also has a default max lifetime for connections to prevent memory bloat on the database itself. This is a random interval for each connection between 30 and 60 minutes. This allows multiple connections to independently come up and down without affecting the service. What a statement takes and returns is learned once for the whole pool, not once per connection, so a new connection never has to ask about a query the pool already knows. Each connection still prepares a statement itself the first time it runs it. Up to `max_pipeline` queries (100 by default) are sent on one connection before the answers come back, which is what makes many small queries fast. A query that waits on a lock holds up those behind it on the same connection; lower `max_pipeline` if that matters more to you than throughput. #### Scheduling A query goes to an idle connection when there is one. When every connection is busy, the pool pipelines it on the connection where it should be done soonest, from how long each statement has taken before and how long what is in flight has been running, so a quick query doesn't wait behind a slow one when another connection is about to be free. Slow queries (around 100 ms or more) are kept together on the connections that already run slow work, within twice their own time, once the rest of the pool is needed for quick work; how many connections that is follows how much quick and slow work has come in over the last few seconds. Nothing has to be configured, and while nothing slow is in flight the pool places queries as before. `scheduler: false` turns it off: a busy pool then pipelines on the connection with the fewest queries in flight. With `max: 1` there is only one connection to choose, so the scheduler is off. #### Pool stats `sql.stats` tells what the pool is doing right now: ```js sql.stats // { connections: 3, opening: 0, idle: 1, leased: 1, waiting: 0 } ``` ### Connection timeout By default, connections will not close until `.end()` is called. However, it may be useful to have them close automatically when: - re-instantiating multiple ` sql`` ` instances - using Postgres.js in a Serverless environment (Lambda, etc.) - using Postgres.js with a database service that automatically closes connections after some time (see [`ECONNRESET` issue](https://github.com/porsager/postgres/issues/179)) This can be done using the `idle_timeout` or `max_lifetime` options. These configuration options specify the number of seconds to wait before automatically closing an idle connection and the maximum time a connection can exist, respectively. For example, to close a connection that has either been idle for 20 seconds or existed for more than 30 minutes: ```js const sql = postgres({ idle_timeout: 20, max_lifetime: 60 * 30 }) ``` ### Cloudflare Workers support Postgres.js runs in Cloudflare Workers on the [TCP socket API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/). Bundlers pick the Workers build through the `workerd` export condition, so the import is the same as anywhere else. You can use Postgres.js directly in a Worker, or to benefit from connection pooling and query caching, via the [Hyperdrive](https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/learning/connect-to-postgres/#driver-examples) service available to Workers by passing the Hyperdrive `connectionString` when creating a new `postgres` client as follows: ```ts import postgres from 'postgres' interface Env { HYPERDRIVE: Hyperdrive } export default { async fetch(req: Request, env: Env, ctx: ExecutionContext) { const sql = postgres(env.HYPERDRIVE.connectionString) const results = await sql`SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10` ctx.waitUntil(sql.end()) return Response.json(results) } } ``` Postgres.js uses `Buffer`, `crypto` and `events` from the Node.js compatibility of Workers, which is on by default from the compatibility date 2026-08-04. For an earlier date, enable it in `wrangler.toml`: ```toml compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"] ``` A few things differ in Workers: - The server certificate is always checked, whatever `ssl` is set to. - `sslnegotiation: 'direct'` is refused with `SSL_NEGOTIATION_NOT_SUPPORTED`, as Workers sockets cannot send ALPN. - Channel binding isn't available, as Workers sockets don't expose the server certificate, so `channel_binding: 'require'` is rejected with `CHANNEL_BINDING_REQUIRED`. - A connection belongs to the request that opened it, so a client made outside `fetch` cannot be shared between requests. ### Auto fetching of array types The built-in types and their arrays are known without asking the server. The first time a query meets a type the pool doesn't know, the pool asks once for the array types and domains that the database has besides those, so an array of an enum or a domain over a built-in type is read and written like its base type; that connection waits for the answer, which is read on another connection. A type made after that, and any type that is neither, is read and written as text, as in v3. With custom types by name, or `eager_types: true`, they are read when the pool starts instead. If the connection reading them fails, the read is tried again after `backoff`, and once `connect_timeout` has passed the connections waiting for it are closed and their queries reject. If you have revoked access to `pg_catalog` this feature will no longer work and will need to be disabled. You can disable this feature by setting `fetch_types` to `false`. ### Environmental variables It is also possible to connect to the database without a connection string or any options. Postgres.js will fall back to the common environment variables used by `psql` as in the table below: ```js const sql = postgres() ``` | Option | Environment Variables | | ------------------ | ------------------------ | | `host` | `PGHOST` | | `port` | `PGPORT` | | `database` | `PGDATABASE` | | `username` | `PGUSERNAME` or `PGUSER` | | `password` | `PGPASSWORD` | | `ssl` | `PGSSLMODE` | | `application_name` | `PGAPPNAME` | | `idle_timeout` | `PGIDLE_TIMEOUT` | | `connect_timeout` | `PGCONNECT_TIMEOUT` | ### Prepared statements Prepared statements will automatically be created for any queries where it can be inferred that the query is static. This can be disabled by using the `prepare: false` option, which is what a pooler in transaction mode without support for prepared statements needs (see below). With `prepare: false` a query with parameters is described before it runs, as in v3, which costs a round trip, but always uses the types the server has now. A prepared statement keeps the parameter types it was prepared with, on the server and here, and each connection reads rows and writes values only by what its own server described. If a column changes type so that a query no longer fits them, the query fails before it runs; Postgres.js then runs the query once more with a fresh description and prepares the statement again with the new types, unless it was sent in a transaction or on a reserved connection, where the error is returned and the next query is prepared afresh. Once any connection sees a statement describe differently, the other connections prepare it again before they next use it. Where the server can still cast the old parameter type to the new one, such as `json` to `text`, on a connection that has not yet seen the change, there is no error to act on, and the value is stored as that cast gives it; use `prepare: false` if columns change type while the application runs. ### Connection poolers Postgres.js is tested through PgBouncer in session mode and in transaction mode, with and without its support for prepared statements. | Pooler mode | Options | What does not work | | ----------- | ------- | ------------------ | | Session | none | Nothing, apart from what the pooler itself refuses | | Transaction, with [`max_prepared_statements`](https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html#max_prepared_statements) (PgBouncer 1.21+) | none | `LISTEN`, and `DEALLOCATE` sent as SQL | | Transaction, without | `prepare: false` | `LISTEN`, and named prepared statements | In both transaction modes a session belongs to a client only for the length of a transaction, so anything that has to outlive one, like `SET`, `LISTEN` or a temporary table, only works inside `sql.begin` or not at all. Use a direct connection, or a pooler in session mode, for `sql.listen` and `sql.subscribe`. With `max_prepared_statements`, PgBouncer keeps one prepared statement on each server connection for every query text and set of parameter types, shared by all its clients. After a column changes type, a connection may be handed the statement prepared before the change, which still describes the old parameter types; where the server can cast the old type to the new one, there is no error to act on. Use `prepare: false` through PgBouncer if columns change type while the application runs. PgBouncer refuses startup parameters it does not know, so a `connection` option like `{ 'some.var': 1 }` needs [`ignore_startup_parameters`](https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html#ignore_startup_parameters) or `SET` inside a transaction instead. The pid in `state` is the pooler's, not the server's, so `pg_terminate_backend(state.pid)` does not end the session. Supavisor before 2.10, the pooler behind Supabase's port 6543, hangs on pipelined queries in transaction mode: the queries are sent but their answers never arrive. Use `max_pipeline: 1` there until you are on 2.10 or later. Setting `query_timeout` also keeps a pooler that stops answering from hanging the application: the queries reject with `QUERY_TIMEOUT` and the pool connects again. ## Custom Types You can add ergonomic support for custom types, or simply use `sql.typed(value, type)` inline, where type is the PostgreSQL `oid` for the type and the correctly serialized string. _(`oid` values for types can be found in the `pg_catalog.pg_type` table.)_ Adding Query helpers is the cleanest approach which can be done like this: ```js const sql = postgres({ types: { rect: { // The pg_types oid to pass to the db along with the serialized value. to : 1337, // An array of pg_types oids to handle when parsing values coming from the db. from : [1337], //Function that transform values before sending them to the db. serialize : ({ x, y, width, height }) => [x, y, width, height], // Function that transforms values coming from the db. parse : ([x, y, width, height]) => { x, y, width, height } } } }) // Now you can use sql.typed.rect() as specified above const [custom] = await sql` insert into rectangles ( name, rect ) values ( 'wat', ${ sql.typed.rect({ x: 13, y: 37, width: 42, height: 80 }) } ) returning * ` // custom = { name: 'wat', rect: { x: 13, y: 37, width: 42, height: 80 } } ``` A type whose oid isn't fixed, such as one from an extension, can be given by name instead, with `schema.name` allowed. Names are looked up when the pool starts, along with the type's array type, and queries wait for that. A name that doesn't exist rejects queries with `TYPE_NOT_FOUND`, and the lookup is tried again a second later, so a type created afterwards is found. Types by name need `fetch_types`. ```js const sql = postgres({ types: { vector: { to : 'vector', from : ['vector'], serialize : x => '[' + x.join(',') + ']', parse : x => JSON.parse(x) } } }) await sql`insert into items ${ sql({ embedding: sql.typed.vector([1, 2, 3]) }) }` ``` ### Custom socket Easily do in-process ssh tunneling to your database by providing a custom socket for Postgres.js to use. The function (optionally async) is called with the options and the host and port to connect to, and must return a socket-like duplex stream. If the socket has done TLS itself, set `negotiated: true` on it so Postgres.js does not ask the server for TLS again. Here's a sample using [ssh2](https://github.com/mscdex/ssh2) ```js import ssh2 from 'ssh2' const sql = postgres({ ...options, socket: ({ host: [host], port: [port] }) => new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const ssh = new ssh2.Client() ssh .on('error', reject) .on('ready', () => ssh.forwardOut('127.0.0.1', 12345, host, port, (err, socket) => err ? reject(err) : resolve(socket) ) ) .connect(sshOptions) }) }) ``` ## Teardown / Cleanup To ensure proper teardown and cleanup on server restarts use `await sql.end()` before `process.exit()`. `await sql.close()` closes every connection once the queries on it have finished, but leaves the pool usable: the next query opens a connection again. Calling `sql.end()` will reject new queries and return a Promise which resolves when all queries are finished and the underlying connections are closed. If a `{ timeout }` option is provided any pending queries will be rejected once the timeout (in seconds) is reached and the connections will be destroyed. `await using` ends the pool when it goes out of scope: ```js { await using sql = postgres() await sql`select 1` } // sql.end() has been awaited here ``` For scripts that should exit when their work is done, without calling `sql.end()`, `unref_sockets: true` stops idle connections from keeping the process alive, like `allowExitOnIdle` in node-postgres. Connections with queries in flight still do. With `min`, the pool keeps that many connections open once it has been used, and `idle_timeout` closes connections only above that number. `sql.close()` lets them close; the next query opens them again. #### Sample shutdown using [Prexit](https://github.com/porsager/prexit) ```js import prexit from 'prexit' prexit(async () => { await sql.end({ timeout: 5 }) await new Promise(r => server.close(r)) }) ``` ## Reserving connections ### `await sql.reserve()` The `reserve` method pulls out a connection from the pool, and returns a client that wraps the single connection. This can be used for running queries on an isolated connection. ```ts const reserved = await sql.reserve() await reserved`select * from users` await reserved.release() ``` ### `reserved.release()` Once you have finished with the reserved connection, call `release` to add it back to the pool. `using reserved = await sql.reserve()` releases it when it goes out of scope. ## Tracing Postgres.js publishes what it does on Node.js [diagnostics channels](https://nodejs.org/api/diagnostics_channel.html), so a tracer or a metrics library can follow every query without an option or a wrapper. Nothing is published while nobody subscribes, and a query costs nothing measurable then. Diagnostics channels are there on Node.js, Bun and Cloudflare Workers. | Channel | Kind | Published for | | ------- | ---- | ------------- | | `postgres:query` | [tracing channel](https://nodejs.org/api/diagnostics_channel.html#class-tracingchannel) | Every query, from when it is sent off until it settles | | `postgres:connect` | tracing channel | Every attempt to connect to a host, up to a ready connection or an error | | `postgres:transaction` | tracing channel | Every `sql.begin`, up to its commit or rollback | | `postgres:pool` | channel | Connections opening, going idle, being leased and released, closing, and queries waiting | | `postgres:notice` | channel | Every notice from the server | A tracing channel publishes `start` and `end` around the sending of the query, `error` if it fails, and `asyncStart` and `asyncEnd` when it settles, all with the same context object, which fills in as the query goes along. `start` runs in the async context of the code that made the query, so a span started there gets the right parent. #### `postgres:query` | Field | | | ----- | - | | `query` | The text sent, with `$1`, `$2` for the parameters | | `parameters` | The values, only with `debug: true` | | `statement` | The name it is prepared as, `''` if unnamed | | `database`, `user` | As connected with | | `connection`, `host`, `port` | The connection it ran on, once sent | | `command`, `count` | The command tag and the number of rows, once done | | `queued`, `sent`, `firstByte`, `complete` | Times in milliseconds from `performance.now()` | | `result`, `error` | What it resolved or rejected with | #### `postgres:connect` `host`, `port`, `path`, `database`, `user`, `ssl` and `sslnegotiation`, then `result` with the backend `pid`, `status`, `readOnly` and `standby`, or `error`. #### `postgres:transaction` `mode`, `database`, `user`, `connection`, `host`, `port`, and `outcome`: `'commit'`, `'rollback'` or `'prepare'`. #### `postgres:pool` and `postgres:notice` Pool messages have an `event` (`open`, `idle`, `wait`, `lease`, `release` or `close`), the `connection`, `host`, `port` and `database`, and the pool's `stats` at that moment. `lease` and `release` also have the `kind` of lease and `lease` how many milliseconds it `waited`; `close` has the `error`. Notices come as `{ notice, connection, host, port, database }`. #### OpenTelemetry Spans following the [semantic conventions for PostgreSQL](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/db/postgresql/) take a few lines: ```js import dc from 'node:diagnostics_channel' import { trace, SpanKind, SpanStatusCode } from '@opentelemetry/api' const tracer = trace.getTracer('postgres.js') const spans = new WeakMap() dc.tracingChannel('postgres:query').subscribe({ start(x) { spans.set(x, tracer.startSpan(x.database, { kind: SpanKind.CLIENT, attributes: { 'db.system.name': 'postgresql', 'db.namespace': x.database, 'db.query.text': x.query ?? undefined } })) }, error(x) { const span = spans.get(x) span.recordException(x.error) span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR, message: x.error.message }) span.setAttribute('error.type', x.error.code || x.error.name) x.error.severity && span.setAttribute('db.response.status_code', x.error.code) }, asyncEnd(x) { const span = spans.get(x) span.setAttributes({ 'db.query.text': x.query ?? undefined, 'db.operation.name': x.command ?? undefined, 'db.response.returned_rows': x.count ?? undefined, 'server.address': x.host ?? undefined, 'server.port': x.port ?? undefined }) x.command && span.updateName(x.command + ' ' + x.database) span.end() }, end() {}, asyncStart() {} }) ``` #### Metrics ```js import dc from 'node:diagnostics_channel' dc.subscribe('tracing:postgres:query:asyncEnd', x => { histogram.record(x.complete - x.queued, { command: x.command, error: !!x.error }) }) dc.subscribe('postgres:pool', x => { gauge.record(x.stats.waiting) }) ``` ## Error handling Errors are all thrown to related queries and never globally. Errors coming from database itself are always in the [native Postgres format](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/errcodes-appendix.html), and the same goes for any [Node.js errors](https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html#errors_common_system_errors) eg. coming from the underlying connection. The stack of a query error leads to the line in your code that made the query, not into Postgres.js, even when the error comes back long after it was sent. Query errors will also contain the `query` string and the `parameters`. These are not enumerable to avoid accidentally leaking confidential information in logs. To log these it is required to specifically access `error.query` and `error.parameters`, or set `debug: true` in options. An error from the server is a `PostgresError`, with the fields of the server's [error message](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/protocol-error-fields.html) as properties: ```js import postgres, { PostgresError } from 'postgres' try { await sql`insert into users ${ sql(user) }` } catch (error) { if (error instanceof PostgresError && error.code === '23505') return { taken: error.constraint_name } throw error } ``` | Property | | | --- | --- | | `code` | The [SQLSTATE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/errcodes-appendix.html), such as `'23505'` for a unique violation | | `message`, `severity`, `severity_local` | Always there | | `detail`, `hint`, `position`, `where` | When the server sends them | | `schema_name`, `table_name`, `column_name`, `data_type_name`, `constraint_name` | For errors about a specific object | | `file`, `line`, `routine` | Where in the server it happened | | `query`, `parameters`, `types` | The query that failed; not enumerable unless `debug` is on | `JSON.stringify(error)` includes the message and every enumerable field. Errors from the connection are Node.js errors such as `ECONNREFUSED`, or one with a `code` from the list below. Every error Postgres.js throws has a `code`. There are also the following errors specifically for this library. ##### UNSAFE_TRANSACTION > Only use sql.begin, sql.reserved or max: 1 To ensure statements in a transaction runs on the same connection (which is required for them to run inside the transaction), you must use [`sql.begin(...)`](#transactions), a [reserved connection](#reserving-connections) or only allow a single connection in options (`max: 1`). A query on the pool that leaves its connection in a transaction is rolled back and rejected with this error. A query that looks like it may start a transaction runs alone on its connection, so no other query ends up in it, and one that opens and closes its own transaction, such as a migration file with `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`, runs as it is. ##### UNDEFINED_VALUE > Undefined values are not allowed Postgres.js won't accept `undefined` as values in tagged template queries since it becomes ambiguous what to do with the value. If you want to set something to null, use `null` explicitly. ##### MESSAGE_NOT_SUPPORTED > X (X) is not supported Whenever a message is received from Postgres which is not supported by this library. Feel free to file an issue if you think something is missing. ##### PROTOCOL_ERROR > The server sent a message with an invalid length (-1) The server, or something between it and Postgres.js, sent a message whose length is below 4 bytes or above 1 GiB. The connection is closed, and its queries reject with this error or with a connection error caused by it. ##### NUL_CHARACTER > The connection parameter database contains a NUL character A connection parameter such as `database`, `user` or `application_name` contains `\0`. The startup message separates parameters with NUL, so the rest would be read as more parameters; the connection is refused instead. ##### MAX_PARAMETERS_EXCEEDED > Max number of parameters (65534) exceeded The postgres protocol doesn't allow more than 65534 (16bit) parameters. If you run into this issue there are various workarounds such as using `sql([...])` to escape values instead of passing them as parameters. ##### SASL_SIGNATURE_MISMATCH > Message type X not supported When using SASL authentication the server responds with a signature at the end of the authentication flow which needs to match the one on the client. This is to avoid [man-in-the-middle attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-in-the-middle_attack). If you receive this error the connection was canceled because the server did not reply with the expected signature. ##### NOT_TAGGED_CALL > Query not called as a tagged template literal Making queries has to be done using the sql function as a [tagged template](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals#Tagged_templates). This is to ensure parameters are serialized and passed to Postgres as query parameters with correct types and to avoid SQL injection. ##### AUTH_TYPE_NOT_IMPLEMENTED > Authentication type X is not supported Postgres supports many different authentication types. This one is not supported. Cleartext, MD5, SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS are. ##### AUTHENTICATION_INCOMPLETE > The server was ready before it accepted the authentication The server said it was ready for queries before it had accepted the password, for example in the middle of a SCRAM exchange or without asking for authentication at all. The connection is refused, so authentication can not be skipped by something between the client and the server. ##### SASL_MECHANISM_NOT_SUPPORTED / SASL_NONCE_MISMATCH The server offered no SASL mechanism Postgres.js supports (SCRAM-SHA-256 or, over TLS, SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS), or its answer did not continue the client's nonce, which means something between them interfered. ##### CHANNEL_BINDING_REQUIRED > channel_binding is require, but the server did not offer it `channel_binding` is `'require'`, and the connection could not be bound to the server's certificate: it is not over TLS, the server did not offer SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS, asked for a cleartext or MD5 password (which is then not sent) or authenticated without SCRAM, or the certificate could not be hashed for it. ##### SSL_NOT_SUPPORTED > The server does not support SSL connections `ssl` was `require` or stricter and the server has no TLS. ##### SSL_NEGOTIATION_NOT_SUPPORTED `sslnegotiation: 'direct'` was asked for in Cloudflare Workers, which cannot do it. ##### TRANSACTION_ROLLED_BACK > The server rolled back the transaction instead of committing it `sql.begin` sent COMMIT and the server answered that it rolled back instead, so nothing in the transaction was saved. > The query was not sent, the transaction was rolled back with sql.rollback() A query, savepoint or nested `sql.begin` was made after `sql.rollback()` in the same transaction or savepoint. ##### ARRAY_REMOVED > sql.array() is removed in v4, pass the array as it is Arrays are typed from what they hold, so they need no helper. Add a cast where the server should treat it as something else, like `${ ids }::int[]`. ##### CONNECTION_CLOSED > write CONNECTION_CLOSED host:port This error is thrown if the connection was closed without an error. This should not happen during normal operations, so please create an issue if this was unexpected. ##### CONNECTION_ENDED > write CONNECTION_ENDED host:port This error is thrown if the user has called [`sql.end()`](#teardown--cleanup) and performed a query afterward. ##### CONNECTION_DESTROYED > write CONNECTION_DESTROYED host:port This error is thrown for any queries that were pending when the timeout to [`sql.end({ timeout: X })`](#teardown--cleanup) was reached. ##### QUEUE_TIMEOUT > Waited more than 5 seconds for a connection A query, transaction or reserve waited longer than `queue_timeout` for a connection. It was never sent. ##### QUERY_TIMEOUT > The query did not finish within query_timeout (5 seconds) A query took longer than `query_timeout`, waiting and running together, and was canceled. Its `cause` is the `57014` it was canceled with, or `CANCEL_UNANSWERED` when the server didn't answer the cancel, in which case whether the query ran is unknown. ##### CANCEL_UNANSWERED > The server did not answer within cancel_timeout (5 seconds) after a query was canceled, so whether it ran is unknown The `cause` of `CONNECTION_DESTROYED` or `QUERY_TIMEOUT` for the queries on a connection that was closed because a cancel request got no answer within `cancel_timeout`. Whether those queries ran is unknown, as when a connection is lost. ##### TYPE_NOT_FOUND > The type vector does not exist A custom type given by name was not found when the pool looked it up. ##### NESTED_TRANSACTION_MODE > A nested transaction runs in a savepoint, which can not change the transaction mode A nested `sql.begin` was given a mode other than its transaction's, or called `sql.prepare()`. ##### TLS_HANDSHAKE_FAILED > The TLS connection to host:port was lost before the server answered On Cloudflare Workers: the TLS handshake could not be completed, most often because the server's certificate is not signed by a publicly trusted CA. Workers always verify the certificate; Hyperdrive connects to such servers for you. ##### NO_COLUMNS > The insert helper got no columns An insert or update helper was given an empty object or an empty list of columns, which would make invalid SQL. ##### NO_PARTS > sql.identifier needs at least one part `sql.identifier()` was called with no parts, which would leave the name out of the query. ##### BATCH_NOT_ARRAY / BATCH_NOT_QUERY / BATCH_EXECUTED / BATCH_UNSUPPORTED > sql.batch takes an array of queries [`sql.batch`](#batches) was given something it can not send. `BATCH_NOT_ARRAY`: the argument is not an array. `BATCH_NOT_QUERY`: an item is not a query made with `sql`, such as a string, or what `.readable()`, `.writable()` or `.cursor()` without a callback return. `BATCH_EXECUTED`: an item has already run, because it was awaited, is a `.forEach()`, which starts at once, or was in another batch. `BATCH_UNSUPPORTED`: an item is a `.describe()` or a `.cursor(fn)`. The message names the position of the item. These are thrown by the `sql.batch()` call itself, before anything is sent, so `sql.batch(queries).catch(...)` does not catch them; `await` it inside `try`. ##### CONNECT_TIMEOUT > write CONNECT_TIMEOUT host:port This error is thrown if the startup phase of the connection (tcp, protocol negotiation, and auth) took more than the default 30 seconds or what was specified using `connect_timeout` or `PGCONNECT_TIMEOUT`. ##### COPY_IN_PROGRESS > You cannot execute queries during copy This error is thrown if trying to run a query during a copy operation (writable / readable). ## TypeScript support `postgres` has TypeScript support. You can pass a row list type for your queries in this way: ```ts interface User { id: number name: string } const users = await sql`SELECT * FROM users` users[0].id // ok => number users[1].name // ok => string users[0].invalid // fails: `invalid` does not exists on `User` ``` However, be sure to check the array length to avoid accessing properties of `undefined` rows: ```ts const users = await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` if (!users.length) throw new Error('Not found') return users[0] ``` You can also prefer destructuring when you only care about a fixed number of rows. In this case, we recommend you to prefer using tuples to handle `undefined` properly: ```ts const [user]: [User?] = await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` if (!user) // => User | undefined throw new Error('Not found') return user // => User // NOTE: const [first, second]: [User?] = await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` // fails: `second` does not exist on `[User?]` const [first, second] = await sql<[User?]>`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` // don't fail : `second: User | undefined` ``` The types that matter are also exported by name: ```ts import postgres, { type Sql, type TransactionSql, type Row } from 'postgres' function users(sql: Sql) { return sql`select * from users` } ``` A function that should run on the pool, in a transaction or on a reserved connection alike takes `ISql`, which is what the three have in common: ```ts import postgres, { type ISql } from 'postgres' function users(sql: ISql) { return sql`select * from users` } await users(sql) await sql.begin(sql => users(sql)) ``` `PostgresError` is exported by name too, so `import { PostgresError } from 'postgres'` works with `instanceof`. The types are checked against a test of their own with TypeScript 4.9 and later. Feel free to open an issue if you have trouble with types. ## Upgrading from v3 The API is the same as v3's, and most code runs unchanged. Check these before upgrading. ### Parameter types are decided by the server v3 typed a `Date` as `timestamptz`, a boolean as `boolean`, a `Buffer` as `bytea`, a `bigint` as `int8` and arrays of these by their first element. v4 sends them without a type and the server decides from the query (see [Parameter types](#parameter-types)). `infer: true` keeps v3's behaviour: ```js const sql = postgres({ infer: true }) ``` Nothing changes for `timestamptz` columns, for values written to a column of their own type, for strings and numbers, or for anything with a cast. What does change: **Dates and times outside UTC.** When the session's `TimeZone` or the Node.js process isn't UTC: - A `Date` written to a `timestamp` column, or compared with one, is taken as UTC instead of the session's local time. - A `Date` written to a `date` column, compared with one or cast with `::date`, takes the day in UTC instead of in the session's time zone, so near midnight it can be a day off. - A `timestamp` column is read as UTC instead of the process's local time, so rows v3 wrote as local time are read back shifted by the UTC offset. This query shows whether that concerns you: ```sql select current_setting('TimeZone') as session_time_zone, table_schema, table_name, column_name, data_type from information_schema.columns where data_type in ('timestamp without time zone', 'date', 'time without time zone') and table_schema not in ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema') ``` If it returns no columns, or the time zone is `UTC` and so is your Node.js process (`TZ=UTC`, the default in most containers), nothing changes. Otherwise use `infer: true`, or move those columns to `timestamptz`, or cast the parameters (`${ date }::timestamptz`). **Errors that need a cast.** A `Date` given where the query doesn't decide its type is now an error from the server, with the fix in the query: | Query | Error | With a cast | | ----- | ----- | ----------- | | ``date_trunc('day', ${ date })``, `extract`, `to_char`, `to_json`, `jsonb_build_object` | `42725` function is not unique, or `42P18` / `42804` could not determine the type | `${ date }::timestamptz` | | ``${ date } + interval '1 day'`` | `22007` invalid input syntax for type interval | `${ date }::timestamptz + interval '1 day'` | | A `Date` written to a `time` column | `22007` invalid input syntax for type time | `${ date }::timestamptz::time` | | ``${ 2n ** 60n } + 1`` | `22003` out of range for type integer | `${ n }::int8 + 1` | **Values that come back as text.** A boolean, `Date`, `Buffer` or array that is only selected back, as in ``select ${ true } as x``, comes back as a string, since the server reads it as text; cast it to get the type back. A `Buffer` written to a `text` column is stored as its text instead of `\x` hex, a `Date` written to a `text` column as an ISO string ending in `Z`, and `${ 10n } + 1` gives the number `11` instead of the string `'11'`. A string such as `'yes'` or `'t'` for a `boolean` is now read by the server as `true`; v3 wrote any string for a `boolean` as `false`. **One more round trip.** A query whose parameters are all dates, booleans, `bigint`s, `Buffer`s or arrays of these is described before its first run on each connection, as queries with strings and numbers already were. ### Everything else - **Runtimes.** Node.js 18 or later, Bun and Cloudflare Workers; Deno runs the npm package. Postgres.js is an ES module; `require('postgres').default` works on Node.js 20.19 and 22.12 and later. - **`sql.array()` is removed.** Pass the array as it is, with a cast where the query doesn't decide its type: `${ ids }::int[]`. - **Transactions are stricter.** A `COMMIT` the server answers with `ROLLBACK` rejects with `TRANSACTION_ROLLED_BACK`, a query on a transaction or reserved connection after it ended rejects, a query that can't be built inside a transaction aborts it, and a `begin` sent outside `sql.begin`, a reserved connection or `max: 1` rejects with `UNSAFE_TRANSACTION` and is rolled back. - **Domains** are read and written as their base type, so a domain over `int[]` comes back as an array of numbers. - **`infinity` timestamps** are `Infinity` and `-Infinity` instead of an invalid `Date`. - **TypeScript.** The types are an ES module with a default export and named types: `import postgres, { type Sql } from 'postgres'`.
